## The hill gets a sky

v1.5.14 put three riders on the hill and took the lift away. This one
is about everything *around* them — the sky, the trees, the weather —
and about two creatures whose arms turned out not to be attached to
their bodies.

### Aurora

The single biggest visual change in this release, and it exists because
of a fact about the panel rather than in spite of one.

This display quantises blue to four levels. A blue sky gradient can only
ever show four flat steps, which is why the night sky had to be dithered
row by row in v1.5.14 just to stop being stripes. But **green and red
each get eight levels** — and an aurora is almost entirely green with a
warm base. It is the one large soft thing this hardware can actually
render, and every other atmospheric effect on this hill has been fought
through the four-step ramp to get there.

Two ribbons snake sideways as they descend, on different periods, green
through the body and warming to red at the lower edge. Drawn as
horizontal rows rather than vertical curtains, because a ribbon is one
line call per row where a curtain is several per column — about seventy
calls against two hundred for the same band of sky. It fades out at dawn
and in heavy weather, and swells on a slow cycle so it is not always at
full strength.

### Wind you can see

There was already wind in the snow. The trees ignored it entirely. Now
they bend — and the offset **grows with height**, which is the whole
trick: a uniform shift reads as three tiers sliding sideways, a
height-weighted one reads as a trunk bending. Far trees move a little,
the big foreground pine moves a lot, so the wind has depth too.

Costs nothing. It moves rectangles that were already being drawn.

### Snow that lands and stays

Snow used to fall past the trees. It **builds up on the branches** now,
each tree catching at its own rate so the hillside whitens tree by tree
instead of all at once — a hillside where every tree turns white on the
same frame reads as a palette swap. A heavily loaded tree dumps the lot
in one go rather than fading back down, because that is what actually
happens and it reads far better.

### Somebody finally falls over

Every jump used to land perfectly. One in five goes wrong now — one in
three off a spin, since he is facing the wrong way when the snow
arrives. Skis one way, poles another, hat in the air, a puff of snow.

Then **he lies there for a second and a half**. Nothing moves. That
stillness is the joke: a crash that resolves in four frames reads as a
glitch, and one that holds reads as a person having a bad time. Only
once he has stopped moving does the bubble come up — *"oof"*, *"ow."*,
*"\*crunch\*"*, *"I'm fine"*, *"worth it"*, *"my skis"*, *"send it"*,
*"did you see"*.

**This also fixed the jumps.** The ramp test was a position window, and
the ramp moves left while the rider moves right — they close about three
pixels a frame, and fourteen on a long one, straight over a six-pixel
window without ever being inside it. Riders were sailing past ramps with
nothing happening. It is a crossing test now, so a jump is a jump.

### A lodge on the ridge

Two storeys with a stepped roofline, log courses, snow-loaded overhangs,
a lit door spilling onto the snow, and a chimney whose smoke leans on
the same wind as the trees. Five windows, and **every one runs its own
brightness cycle** off a hash of its index — one has a fire in it and
flickers, each goes dark for a while now and then when somebody goes to
bed, and bright ones throw warm light onto the wall below. A row of
windows at one brightness reads as a decal; the same row varying
independently reads as a building with people in it.

The periods are long on purpose. At two to seven seconds this read as a
string of fairy lights; at six to seventeen it reads as rooms.

### The yeti was in pieces

His legs were not attached to his body. The torso ended three pixels
above where the legs began, and worse, when he leaned — winded, or
recoiling from a ski pole — the torso moved and the legs did not, so
his whole upper half slid six pixels off them.

His arms were worse. Two near-black bars floating five pixels off a
pale grey body, with their top two rows above the torso entirely.

Both fixed. He has hips now that move with him. And he has **real arms
— shoulder, elbow, hand** — with a furry upper arm that emerges from the
body rather than being bolted to the side of it, only going dark at the
forearm. When he runs, the whole arm ripples: the elbow leads and the
hand lags a quarter-cycle behind, which is what reads as loose rather
than merely fast. His feet swing too, and the trailing one lifts.

### The Inspection

The eat runs about one chase in six, so it has to be worth having waited
for. It used to be grab, lift, chomp — the yeti being fast.

Now he **catches the rider, raises him to eye level, holds him there and
looks at him**, turns him over to check the other side, and only then
eats him. The pause is the whole joke, and a pause is the one thing the
old version had none of. His mouth stays shut while he is looking; the
jaw only opens once he has decided. The rider's struggling drops to
almost nothing once he is up there — he has worked out how this ends —
and his eyes go from wide to flat resignation, two pixels of difference
doing all the work.

**And they talk.** While he is being examined — yeti: *"hm."*, *"let me
see"*, *"checks out"*, *"no lift pass"*. Rider: *"hi."*, *"sir?"*, *"I'm
mostly bone"*, *"we can talk"*. When he decides — yeti: *"yep"*, *"five
stars"*, *"mm"*, *"worth the run"*. Rider: *"oh COME on"*, *"not the
face"*, *"tell my dog"*, *"bye"*.

There is an actual dog on that hill.

A snowboarder gets eaten in his own jacket, with his own board sticking
out. Previously everyone was eaten as a skier.

### Two more things

**The werewolf's speech bubble is on top now.** It was drawn by the FIRE
background, and the mascot is painted over the background afterwards —
so the bubble was landing behind Squachy. It is handed forward and drawn
after him, the same way ALL CLEAR already is.

**Powder off the edges.** A rider carving hard throws a small rooster
tail off the uphill edge. It scales with the turn, so it comes and goes
with the carve rather than trailing him like an exhaust.

### The actually-useful part
- **Added**: an aurora over the ridge
- **Added**: wind bends the trees, with the offset growing with height
- **Added**: snow accumulates on branches and sheds when heavy
- **Added**: riders can crash on landing, lie still, and say something about it
- **Added**: a lodge on the far ridge with independently lit windows
- **Added**: powder spray off a hard carve
- **Changed**: the eat is an inspection now — he looks at you first, and both of you have lines
- **Fixed**: jumps were silently not firing at real frame rates
- **Fixed**: the yeti's legs and arms were not attached to his body
- **Fixed**: the yeti's arms are jointed and animate
- **Fixed**: the rider had no voice during the one sequence with the best lines
- **Fixed**: the werewolf's speech bubble was hidden behind Squachy
- **Fixed**: a snowboarder was eaten as a skier
